lesson.title: G1: The Cell's Growth and Decision Phase
lesson.summary: G1 is the first gap phase of interphase, when the cell grows, produces proteins and organelles, and passes through a critical checkpoint that decides whether it commits to dividing.
lesson.body:
G1 stands for "Gap 1," a somewhat unfortunate name because it makes the phase sound like empty time between more important events. It is not. G1 begins immediately after a cell finishes dividing and is, for most cells, the longest and most metabolically active phase of the entire cell cycle. During G1 the cell grows in physical size, synthesizes the proteins and RNA it will need for the phases ahead, and duplicates organelles like mitochondria. At this point each chromosome in the cell is still a single, unreplicated structure, and the total chromosome number matches whatever is normal for that species, 46 in humans. The DNA has not yet been copied, that happens next, in S phase.

Late in G1, the cell passes through a critical checkpoint, sometimes called the restriction point, where it evaluates whether it is actually ready to commit to dividing. The checkpoint checks things like whether the cell has grown large enough, whether nutrients and growth factor signals are adequate, and whether the DNA is free of detectable damage. If conditions look favorable, internal signaling proteins called cyclins and their partner enzymes, cyclin-dependent kinases, push the cell past the checkpoint and into S phase. If conditions are not favorable, the cell can instead exit the cycle into G0, the quiescent state introduced in the cell cycle overview, and simply not divide until conditions improve, or, for cells like mature neurons, not divide again at all.

This checkpoint matters because committing to divide is expensive and, if done under the wrong conditions, dangerous. A cell that starts copying its DNA before it has the resources to finish, or that copies DNA that is already damaged, risks producing daughter cells with an incomplete or corrupted genome. By pausing here and checking first, the cell avoids wasting resources on a division it cannot properly complete and avoids passing damaged genetic material on to its offspring.
